Seminar 9: Text-as-Data Methods in Political Science

Author

Zach Dickson

Start here:

This notebook provides an example of how to use text-as-data methods in R. There are three example datasets provided in the data folder: Reddit posts on climate change (reddit_climate_change_2022_sample.csv), Parliament oral questions from PMQs (commons_oral_questions.csv), and UK Green Party Press Releases (uk_green_party_press_releases.csv). There are two different methods demonstrated in this notebook: dictionary-based methods and sentiment analysis. You can choose one or both methods to apply to your data.

  • Step 1:
    • Choose a dataset to analyze. You can use one of the provided datasets or bring your own text data.
  • Step 2:
    • Choose a method to apply to the data: dictionary-based methods or sentiment analysis.
  • Step 3:
    • Apply the chosen method to the data and analyze the results.
# install packages if they are not already installed

# List of package names to install
packages_to_install <- c('tidyverse', 'sentimentr', 'wordcloud2')

# Check if each package is already installed
for (package_name in packages_to_install) {
  if (!(package_name %in% installed.packages())) {
    # If not installed, install the package
    install.packages(package_name)
  }
}

Make a word cloud of the text column

# convert all text to one big string
text <- paste(data$text, collapse = " ")
# create a word frequency table
word_freq <- table(strsplit(text, "\\W+"))
# remove some stop words (we could add more to to this list)
stop_words <- c('and', 'a', 'the','I','for','in','it','is', 'on','this', 'be','at','just','or','do','if','how','https','like')
word_freq <- word_freq[!(names(word_freq) %in% stop_words)]
# convert the word frequency table to a data frame
word_freq_df <- as.data.frame(word_freq)
# print the wordcloud using the wordcloud2 package
wordcloud2(word_freq_df, size = 2, backgroundColor = "white")

Text analysis: Dictionary-based method

First, we need to create a dictionary for the analysis by making a list of words that indicate a topic of interest

# Example: Climate Change Dictionary 
climate_change_dictionary <- c('climate', 'environment', 'global warming', 'greenhouse gas', 'carbon', 'emission', 'pollution', 'fossil fuel', 'renewable', 'sustainability', 'ecosystem', 'biodiversity', 'deforestation', 'ocean acidification', 'sea level rise', 'extreme weather', 'heatwave', 'drought', 'flood', 'hurricane')


# create a function to count the number of times the words in the dictionary appear in a given text
count_dictionary_words <- function(text, dictionary) {
  # Convert the text to lowercase
  text <- tolower(text)
  # Split the text into words
  words <- strsplit(text, "\\W+")
  # Count the number of words in the dictionary that appear in the text for each row of the data
  count <- sum(sapply(words, function(word) sum(word %in% dictionary)))
  return(count)
}


# Apply the function to the text column of the data
data$climate_change_count <- sapply(data$text, count_dictionary_words, dictionary = climate_change_dictionary)

# print the value counts of the climate_change_count column
table(data$climate_change_count)

  0   1 
494   6

Plot the number of climate change related words over time

data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = climate_change_count)) +
   geom_smooth() + # we could swith to geom_point() to see the actual data points or geom_line() to see the line connecting the points
  labs(title = "Number of Climate Change Related Words Over Time",
       x = "Date",
       y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'

Sentiment Analysis

We’ll use the Sentimentr package to analyze the sentiment of the text data. Additional details about the library can be found here: https://github.com/trinker/sentimentr.

# use the sentimentr package to calculate the sentiment of the text
sentiment <- sentiment_by(data$text)

# print the first few rows of the sentiment data
head(sentiment)
Key: <element_id>
   element_id word_count    sd ave_sentiment
        <int>      <int> <num>         <num>
1:          1         13    NA    -0.1109400
2:          2          9    NA     0.2666667

5:          5         10    NA     0.0000000
6:          6         12    NA     0.1443376
# plot a histogram of the sentiment scores
hist(sentiment$ave_sentiment)
# add the sentiment scores to the dataset 
data$sentiment <- sentiment$ave_sentiment

# add the word count to the dataset 
data$word_count <- sentiment$word_count 
# plot the sentiment over time using GGplot
data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = sentiment)) +
  geom_smooth() +
  labs(title = "Sentiment Over Time",
       x = "Date",
       y = "Sentiment Score") +
  theme_minimal()
`geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'
